## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization over per-particle components can approach the streaming ceiling on death-free workloads.

## Cache saturation
The ns/particle curve is FLAT across N at every death rate, with no knee at either cache boundary. At q=0.01, cost drops slightly from 8.09 ns/p (N=4000) to 7.542 (N=1M) — pure overhead amortization at small N — then ticks up marginally to 7.593 at N=4M. The L1d spill at N≈963 lies below the smallest measured point, so it is invisible. The L2 spill at N≈61680 falls between N=4000 and N=65000, yet cost does not rise there; it actually falls from 8.09 to 7.622, confirming the algo is not streaming-limited. Death rate raises the floor monotonically — 7.5, 8.3, 9.0, 11.1, 13.4 ns/p at q=0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 — but preserves the flat N-shape at every rate, indicating churn adds per-particle compute cost without introducing a memory bottleneck.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved bandwidth is 9.02 GB/s at q=0.01 and N=262000, which is 35.8% of the 25.22 GB/s streaming ceiling. The algo is compute/overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound: the absence of any cost rise at the L2→DRAM spill proves memory throughput is not the limiter. Bandwidth degrades with death rate — 9.02, 8.23, 7.54, 6.12, 5.07 GB/s at q=0.01 through 0.5 — tracking the rising per-particle branchy-respawn cost rather than any N-dependent memory effect. There is no regime in which the algo transitions toward the streaming ceiling; it plateaus at 36% even in the lowest-churn, largest-N case.

## Assembly
The compiler did vectorize, but component-wise within a single particle, not across particles. The position update uses `fmul.4s v0, v3, v4` and `fadd.4s v0, v1, v0` on four floats packed via `ext.16b v3, v1, v2, #0xc` and `mov.s v3[3], v0[0]`, and the velocity update uses `fmul.2s`/`fadd.2s`. A single `ld1.s {v2}[1], [x8]` is an indexed gather loading one float from a strided offset. This narrow 4-lane vectorization on 68-byte stride-1 particles explains the modest 9 GB/s. The render loop is entirely scalar: 19 `strb` byte stores (`strb w2, [x1]`, `strb w2, [x1, #0x1]`, `strb w2, [x1, #0x2]`) with 18 `csel` clamp sequences and 21 branches, capping throughput well below the ceiling.

## Verdict
Refuted — at q=0.01 the algo sustains only 9.02 GB/s = 36% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling with no cache-spill knee, and component-wise `fmul.4s`/`fadd.4s` vectorization plus scalar `strb` scatter stores cannot close the gap. The flat N-curve (7.54→7.59 ns/p from N=262k to 4M) confirms compute-bound operation, so auto-vectorization over per-particle components does not approach the streaming ceiling even in the death-free regime.
